original_value: Thermal remote sensing provides a method to describe spatial heterogeneity of the “urban heat island” effect and to evaluate the function of temperature regulation. Rapid urbanization and heatwave events with increasing frequencies need a quantitative analysis on the supply and demand for an urban temperature regulating service, which is a gap in urban heat island (UHI) studies in rapidly urbanizing cities. In order to study the quantitative relationship between landscape metrics (including area index and shape index) and temperature regulating service, this study applied a temperature regulating service in an urban thermal environment study based on the “source–sink” landscape theory in western Shenzhen in different periods. The identification of source and sink landscapes is based on the spatial relationship of unusual surface features derived from Landsat-5 and -8 and the consideration of the temperature difference. We found that the source landscapes at different periods provide temperature regulating services for different distances, which directly lead to the difference between the theoretical service value based on the Alternative Cost Method and the actual service value considering demand, changing in the same trend. The results show that the supply distance of temperature regulating services in 2005, 2010, and 2013 is 150 m, 180 m, and 210 m, respectively. The temperature regulating service value is 3.043, 3.273, and 4.308 billion yuan in 2005, 2010, and 2013, which is lower than the estimation value without considering supply and demand (16.638, 23.728, and 37.495 billion yuan, respectively). The value of the temperature regulating service has a positive correlation with the increase of the patch area index. With the gradual complexity of the shape, the service value increases first and then decreases. Moreover, the landscapes with the smallest shape index and area index have the shortest distance for service supplying. The assessment of the temperature regulating service needs to consider the presence of demand landscapes. Furthermore, the interaction of landscapes under different conditions requires further consideration. The setting of the cooling landscape shape and area for mitigating the “urban heat island” effect can provide references to urban planners and policymakers in the practice of urban climate adaptation and regulation.

result.paraphrase: Thermal remote sensing offers a way to characterize the spatial variability of the urban heat island effect and assess temperature regulation. With rapid urbanization and increasingly frequent heatwave events, a quantitative analysis of the supply and demand for urban temperature-regulating services is needed, filling a gap in UHI research in fast-growing cities. To examine the quantitative relationship between landscape metrics, including area index and shape index, and temperature-regulating service, this study applied a source–sink landscape-theory approach to temperature-regulating services in the urban thermal environment of western Shenzhen across different periods. Source and sink landscapes were identified from the spatial relationship of anomalous surface features derived from Landsat-5 and Landsat-8, together with temperature differences. We found that source landscapes in different periods provide temperature-regulating services over different distances, directly causing the gap between the theoretical service value based on the Alternative Cost Method and the actual service value that accounts for demand, both of which change in the same trend. The results show that the service-supply distance for temperature regulation was 150 m, 180 m, and 210 m in 2005, 2010, and 2013, respectively. The temperature-regulating service value was 3.043, 3.273, and 4.308 billion yuan in 2005, 2010, and 2013, respectively, lower than the estimated values without considering supply and demand (16.638, 23.728, and 37.495 billion yuan, respectively). The value of temperature-regulating services is positively correlated with increasing patch area index. As shape becomes more complex, the service value first rises and then falls. In addition, landscapes with the smallest shape and area indices have the shortest service-supply distance. Assessment of temperature-regulating services must take demand landscapes into account. Moreover, interactions among landscapes under different conditions require further attention. Setting the shape and area of cooling landscapes to mitigate the urban heat island effect can offer guidance for urban planners and policymakers in urban climate adaptation and regulation.
